analysis.one_liner: Lets industrial plants upgrade and expand without triggering Clean Air Act pollution-control permits.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Clean Air Act, when a factory, refinery, or power plant makes a physical or operational change that increases pollution, it can be classified as a 'modification' and must install modern pollution controls through the New Source Review permitting program. This bill would narrow that definition in three ways: a change only counts as a modification if the plant's maximum hourly emissions would exceed any single hour in the previous 10 years, and changes designed to improve efficiency, reliability, or safety would be exempt unless the EPA finds they would harm health or the environment. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment Subcommittee, which took no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of large polluting facilities — power plants, refineries, chemical plants, cement kilns and similar 'major emitting facilities' — would avoid New Source Review permits, which require installing modern pollution-control technology and can be costly and slow. The bill's own text describes the covered changes as those designed to reduce pollution per unit of production or to improve reliability and safety, which plant operators often cite when seeking to modernize without new permits.

how_it_helps.text: A change counts as a 'modification' requiring a permit only if the maximum hourly emissions achievable after the change exceed the maximum hourly rate achieved in any single hour of the prior 10 years, a much harder test to trip than the existing rule.

Changes designed to reduce pollution per unit of production, or to restore, maintain, or improve reliability or safety, would be exempt from the modification definition unless the EPA determines the resulting increase in maximum achievable hourly emissions would adversely affect health or the environment.

The definitions of 'construction' and 'modification' for major emitting facilities, including in areas that violate air quality standards (nonattainment areas), would exclude changes that do not cause a significant emissions increase in annual actual emissions, shielding more routine projects from permitting.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on people living downwind of industrial facilities in the form of higher emissions of air pollutants, since more plant changes would escape the review that requires modern pollution controls. The bill includes a backstop: the EPA could still treat an exempted change as a modification if it determines the resulting emissions increase would harm health or the environment, which limits but does not eliminate the public exposure.

drawbacks.text: Industry groups have long argued that New Source Review discourages efficiency, reliability, and safety upgrades by subjecting them to lengthy and expensive permitting, and this bill is written to exempt exactly those projects.

The bill's exceptions are not absolute: it keeps them from applying when the EPA determines the increase in maximum achievable hourly emissions would cause an adverse effect on human health or the environment, so the agency retains a check on the worst cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to industry would be fewer and cheaper permits and easier plant upgrades; the cost would be weaker review of emission increases at major facilities, including in areas that already violate air quality standards, which falls on nearby residents and on air quality generally. The EPA health-and-environment override softens the rollback, but the overall shift of the burden of proof away from permitting is a loss for the public side of the ledger.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and a subcommittee, which never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Morgan Griffith introduced the bill on January 9, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On January 20, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials, where no further action was taken.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who live near power plants, refineries, and other major pollution sources are better off, because the current, stricter standard for triggering pollution-control permits stays in place. The bill's would-be beneficiaries, large industrial emitters, gained nothing since the rollback never advanced.

for.name: Rep. H. Morgan Griffith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to narrow the Clean Air Act's New Source Review modification definition.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the bill stayed in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 20, 2023 and took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to break down; the bill had one Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and never left committee.

industries.industry: Fossil-fuel power plants and other major emitting facilities (refineries, chemical plants, cement kilns, paper mills)
industries.note: The bill would let these facilities make more changes — including efficiency, reliability, and safety projects — without triggering New Source Review permits that require installing modern pollution controls. The industry's gain comes at the cost of weaker emissions review, including in areas that already violate air quality standards.

industries.industry: Emissions control equipment and environmental permitting firms
industries.note: Fewer modifications classified as 'modifications' would mean fewer mandated pollution-control installations and fewer permitting projects. This is a secondary effect compared with the emitters themselves.
